feedback: If a learner says natural infection is simply better: acknowledge both build memory, then surface the risks of the actual disease that vaccination avoids.
If a learner expects one vaccine to protect against everything: use the flu-vaccine-vs-cold case to re-establish specificity.
If a learner cannot say why boosters exist: connect to how protection can wane over time and how re-exposure or a further dose re-strengthens the specific memory response.
activities.intendedInsight: Immunological memory and specificity explain real public-health decisions; natural infection and vaccination use the same memory mechanism, but only vaccination avoids the disease's risks.
learnerActions: Pose genuine public-health questions to an immunologist persona, e.g. 'Why do I need a booster?', 'Is catching the illness naturally better than a vaccine?', 'Are all germs bad?'
Explain your current reasoning and let the persona probe it Socratically and correct myths.
Weigh evidence for vaccination vs natural infection, noting that both build memory but infection carries the disease's own risks.
activities.title: Ask the immunologist: boosters, infection vs vaccination, and friendly microbes

feedback: If a learner labels barriers as adaptive: remind that innate defences are always present and work with no prior exposure to a specific pathogen.
If a learner orders memory before clearance: memory cells are made during the first response and remain after the pathogen is cleared; they are not there before first contact.
If a learner cannot explain the flu-vs-cold case: re-anchor on antigen specificity — memory fits one antigen only.
activities.intendedInsight: The two arms, the division of labour between B and T cells, and the primary/secondary timing can be reasoned about explicitly and transferred to the specificity of vaccine protection.
learnerActions: Categorise features as innate vs adaptive (e.g. skin/mucus barriers, inflammation, phagocytes → innate; B-cell antibodies, T-cell killing, memory → adaptive).
Put the adaptive response steps in order: antigen recognised → matching B cell found → cloned/multiplied → antibodies produced → pathogen cleared → memory cells remain.
Match each cell to its role: B cells = make antibodies; T cells = kill infected body cells.
Interpret a primary-vs-secondary response graph: identify which curve is slow/small (first) and which is fast/large (second) and explain why.
State why a flu vaccine gives no protection against a cold virus.
activities.title: Consolidate: sort, sequence and read the response curve
